record.locator: Proposition 1, equation (5), p.5; proof pp.15–16; pure-SK specialization reconstructed in the long record, Near-ground configurations at a prescribed overlap (#near-ground-overlaps).
record.statement: For pure zero-field Gaussian SK H_n=n^(-1/2) sum_{i<j} J_ij sigma_i sigma_j, every fixed r in [0,1) and epsilon,eta>0 admit K=K(r,epsilon,eta)>0 independent of n, such that with disorder probability at least 1-K exp(-n/K) there exist sigma,tau with |R(sigma,tau)-r|<epsilon and both H_n(sigma)/n,H_n(tau)/n >= P_*-eta, for all n>=1.
record.boundary: Ordinary consequence of the imported landscape theorem, full support and attained Parisi formula. Add a common independent N(0,1/2) offset to match covariance; remove it using its Gaussian tail. Each target overlap is fixed before taking size. No typical-pair law, continuum-simultaneous event, efficient construction, Lean extraction or formal proof acceptance is asserted.

aligned_passages.text: Choose one minimizer supplied by the attained Parisi formula, and apply the full-support theorem to that same coefficient. The external landscape theorem below then applies at every point of its Stieltjes support. For every fixed $r\in[0,1)$ and $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, there is a constant $K=K(r,\varepsilon,\eta)>0$, independent of $n$, such that $$ \mathbb P\left(\exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n: \left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i\tau_i-r\right|<\varepsilon, \quad \frac{H_n(\sigma)}n,\frac{H_n(\tau)}n\ge P_*-\eta\right) \ge1-Ke^{-n/K},\qquad n\ge1. $$ The probability is over the SK couplings; the configurations may depend on them. This is the specialization of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5), p. 5][acz] to the full-support minimizer above. Their theorem applies to each point of its Stieltjes support. Its proof, on pp. 15–16, uses the coupled free energy constrained to a neighbourhood of that overlap, passes to the coupled maximum and applies Gaussian concentration. The coupled maximum approaches $2P_*$, while the unrestricted maximum approaches $P_*$; these two facts force both members of a maximizing pair to be near ground energy. The covariance normalization needs one small adjustment. Writing $R=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$, our Hamiltonian has covariance $nR^2/2-1/2$. Adjoin a common independent Gaussian $C$ of variance $1/2$. Then $\widetilde H_n(\sigma)=H_n(\sigma)+C$ has covariance $n\xi(R)$ with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, as in the cited mixed-spin theorem. Its expected maximum equals that of $H_n$, so its ground-state limit is the same $P_*$. Apply the theorem with energy tolerance $\eta/2$. On $|C|\le\eta n/2$, the resulting pair also satisfies the displayed energy inequalities for $H_n$. The omitted event has probability at most $2e^{-\eta^2n^2/4}$, which can be absorbed into $Ke^{-n/K}$ by enlarging $K$. Since the conclusion for $H_n$ depends only on its couplings, this also removes the auxiliary Gaussian from the probability statement. The pointwise result also gives a simultaneous statement at any fixed positive resolution. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose finitely many centres $r_j\in[0,1)$ whose open $\varepsilon/2$-neighbourhoods cover $[0,1]$. Apply the preceding result at each centre with overlap tolerance $\varepsilon/2$ and energy tolerance $\eta$. A finite union bound gives constants $C,c>0$, depending only on these tolerances, such that $$ \mathbb P\!\left(\forall r\in[-1,1]\ \exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n: |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon,\quad H_n(\sigma)/n,H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta\right) \ge1-Ce^{-cn}. \tag{9.1} $$ Indeed, on the event where every centre has a suitable pair, choose a nearest centre and use the triangle inequality. For negative targets, reverse one spin configuration: the pure two-spin Hamiltonian preserves its energy and changes the overlap's sign. The finite net covers the endpoints as well, with centres strictly below one. There is a useful contrast at a fixed finite size. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1][ACZ] proved infinite support. This need not be full support: the measure $\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-k}\delta_{1-2^{-k}}$ has infinitely many atoms and many gaps. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][Chen] subsequently proved full support and smooth nonnegative density. We follow OpenAI's quantitative proof of the support conclusion and its further strict-positivity result. The feature used twice is a lower bound valid throughout every positive constant interval of an admissible coefficient, without a minimising assumption. **Theorem 1 (full support; quantitative proof following [OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][FS]).** If $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimises $\mathcal P$, then $$ \operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1),\qquad \gamma(t_2)>\gamma(t_1)\quad(0\leq t_10$, with probability tending to one there are configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $|R(\sigma,\tau)-\rho|<\delta$ and both energies at least $n(P_*-\eta)$. This follows from [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Proposition 1, equation (5)][ACZ], using the Gaussian normalisation above. Our purpose is to isolate the spatial moment common to the support and density arguments, explain why it needs an integrated estimate, and identify what survives the local-replacement limit. The conclusions and the quantitative method are those of the cited sources. The proof compares two demands on a gap with two support endpoints. Minimality forces $q$ to agree with time there, with endpoint slopes at most one. On a positive constant interval a quantitative estimate makes $q'$ strictly convex, so its integral is smaller than the interval's length. This contradicts the required change in $q$. After excluding all gaps, the identity $q'=1$ supplies the equation from which the same estimate will force $\gamma'>0$. A qualitative crossing criterion already suffices for a bounded gap. The density argument needs more: an estimate for a local constant replacement that need not minimise, at a time where $q''$ need not vanish, and a positive lower bound that survives the limit. The second aim, in §5, is to follow the support identities to a finite Gaussian observable whose rooted energy a QAOA circuit approximates, then identify the additional concentration input for a measured configuration. These optimisation consequences use full support; strict density positivity is a further analytic conclusion. Readers interested in optimisation may accept Theorem 1 and continue to §5. Sections 2–4 assume Itô calculus and martingale convergence; the circuit construction is a separate imported theorem. Omitted proofs are linked to *From Parisi full support to deterministic QAOA circuits: A long reasoning record*, the [companion edition of 26 October 2026](../long/reasoning-record.md); original-source citations remain beside the imported inputs.

The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model asks us to choose signs that
maximise a random sum of pair interactions. The Parisi formula expresses
the limiting maximum through a nondecreasing function, the **order
parameter**. We explain why a minimising order parameter cannot be
constant on any interval below one.

The proof compares two consequences of a hypothetical gap. Minimality
fixes the values and bounds the slopes of an auxiliary curve at its
endpoints. An analytic estimate makes the derivative strictly convex
between them, leaving too little area to connect the required values.
Initial and terminal gaps need separate arguments. We then return to
the spins: a theorem about their energies gives nearly optimal sign
choices differing on any prescribed positive fraction of positions up to one half,
with arbitrarily small error in that fraction.

We follow the quantitative proof in [OpenAI (2026a)][support-manuscript];
[Hong-Bin Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][chen-support] had already proved
full support by a different method. The estimate used here makes the
final contradiction a direct comparison of areas. We assume algebra
and elementary calculus, and introduce probability and cumulative mass
through calculations. The deeper analytic facts are stated where the
proof needs them. By the end of Sections 1–6, the reader should be able
to reconstruct how minimality and those inputs exclude each kind of gap,
then translate the result into a statement about spin configurations.
Section 7 gives optional calculations and answers to the short questions
in the text; the full analytic proofs remain in the cited sources.

## 6. Return to the spins At a fixed finite size, almost surely the only exact maximisers are a configuration and its global reversal. Indeed, two configurations that are neither equal nor global reversals differ in some pair product. Their energy difference is then a Gaussian with positive variance, so a tie has probability zero; there are only finitely many pairs. Intermediate separations become possible when we allow a small loss per spin and let the system grow. A separate theorem of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5)][acz] applies at each point in the minimiser's support. Combining it with full support: for every fixed overlap $r\in[0,1)$ and tolerances $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, with probability over the couplings tending to one exponentially fast as $n\to\infty$, there exist configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $$ |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon, \qquad H_n(\sigma)/n,\ H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta. $$ If $k$ sites differ, $k/n=(1-R)/2$. The overlap tolerance therefore gives $$ \left|\frac{k}{n}-\frac{1-r}{2}\right|<\frac\varepsilon2. $$ For example, fix an energy loss $\eta>0$ per spin and take $r=1/2$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. With probability tending to one exponentially fast, the same instance has two configurations with energies per spin at least $P_*-\eta$ and a differing-site fraction between $0.24$ and $0.26$. No numerical threshold for $n$ is asserted. At target zero, the differing-site fraction can be arbitrarily close to one half. The pair may depend on the chosen target and the couplings. This is existence for each fixed target, not a statement about typically sampled pairs or a procedure for finding them. The companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§9.3, “Near-ground configurations at a prescribed overlap”](../long/reasoning-record.md#near-ground-overlaps), gives the probability bound, covariance adjustment and exact finite-size comparison. The threshold $P_*-\eta$ refers to the limiting value, whereas an exact maximiser attains its particular finite instance's maximum. **Question 5: use the spin conclusion.** Fix an energy loss $\eta>0$. How can the theorem give two configurations differing on between 69% and 71% of sites, although it is stated for nonnegative overlap targets? Which earlier symmetry is needed? Does the stated theorem also permit the choice $\eta=1/n$? [Answer 5](#answer-5).

shared_bindings.gamma: one attained minimizer gamma_0 in the manuscript pure zero-field SK class U, used for full support and the support-point premise of the ACZ landscape theorem

premise_bindings.rationale: Attainment supplies gamma_0 minimizing the same manuscript Parisi functional. Full support is applied to this gamma_0; the landscape theorem then uses the Stieltjes support of that same minimizer.

The attained gamma_0 belongs to the same class U, so its admissibility accompanies its minimality. Pure zero-field SK and xi(t)=t^2/2 remain the fixed model; the common Gaussian covariance adjustment is retained in the landscape argument.

application.rationale: The long record applies ACZ Proposition 1 to the full-support minimizer and identifies its value using the attained Parisi formula. Attainment is supplied by the separately sourced scalar.minimizer_attainment node (and explained in the long record at #minimizer-attainment); it is not an extra caller premise of the landscape consequence. This records the ordinary same-witness application only. The external landscape theorem and the covariance correction remain necessary inputs; no cross-model Lean transport, checked substitution or formal acceptance is asserted.
